question: One member of the Swiss Federal Council serves as President of the Swiss Confederation for one year at a time. That President chairs the meetings of the Federal Council and represents the federal government externally. How does the presidency affect that member's decision-making power?

options.A: The President carries considerably more decision-making power, because the President chairs the meetings and can act for the Council alone.
options.B: The President gains extra decision-making power in foreign affairs only, as the Confederation's external representative.
options.C: The President has hardly any more decision-making power than the other members of the Federal Council.
options.D: The President gains a casting vote, which breaks any deadlock in the Council in the President's favour.

source_quote: In contrast to other countries, the President of the Confederation in Switzerland has hardly any more decision-making power than the other members of the Federal Council.
notes: Swiss-specific: the rotating presidency is a chairmanship, not a head-of-state office. Traps the German Bundeskanzler and US presidential models.

question: The Federal Chancellor is sometimes referred to in Swiss media as the 'eighth Federal Councillor'. What is the Federal Chancellor's actual role?

options.A: A supporting and advisory role for the Federal Council, rather than a seat in it.
options.B: A voting member of the Federal Council, counted among the seven when decisions are taken.
options.C: The head of state, who represents Switzerland towards foreign governments.
options.D: The head of the Federal Administration, supervising its seven departments.

source_quote: There is often talk of an 'eighth Federal Councillor', the Federal Chancellor, who has a supporting and advisory role for the Federal Council.
notes: The Chancellor is neither head of state (the rotating President) nor head of government (the Federal Council as a collegial body). Common model failure: importing the German Bundeskanzler.

question: When the seven members of the Swiss Federal Council deal with an item of business at their meeting, how do they proceed to a decision?

options.A: The President tables a proposal and the other six members confirm it unless three of them object.
options.B: The members vote first on the available options, and the majority position becomes the Federal Council's decision.
options.C: The item is first referred to the cantons for a consultative vote, and the Federal Council then implements the result.
options.D: The members first seek a common solution, and only vote if they fail to reach one.

source_quote: They discuss the items on the agenda at the Federal Council meeting and seek a common solution. Only if it does not reach a solution, does the Federal Council vote.
notes: Consensus-before-vote is the defining feature of the Swiss collegial executive; no majority-vote casting exists in the normal case.

question: The National Council and the Council of States of the Swiss Parliament take most of their decisions separately. When is a decision of the Federal Assembly final?

options.A: As soon as the National Council has approved it, because it is the larger of the two chambers.
options.B: Only when both chambers reach the same conclusion; otherwise the 'resolution of differences procedure' follows.
options.C: When a simple majority of the members of both chambers added together votes for it.
options.D: When the Federal Council endorses it, since the Federal Council sits between the two chambers.

source_quote: Parliament's decisions are only final if the National Council and the Council of States reach the same conclusion. Otherwise, the two chambers must follow the 'resolution of differences procedure' in an attempt to reach an agreement.
notes: Neither chamber is dominant — a bicameral equal-footing design with no overrider, unlike most second chambers.

question: How many seats does the Council of States, the upper chamber of the Swiss Parliament, have?

options.A: 46 seats
options.B: 52 seats
options.C: 26 seats
options.D: 40 seats

source_quote: The Swiss Parliament has 200 seats in the National Council and 46 seats in the Council of States.
notes: 46 = 20 cantons x 2 seats + 6 former half-cantons x 1 seat. 52 is the intuitive-but-wrong 26 x 2. Sourced from S003 (S026 holds the same content).

question: Which cantons are entitled to only one seat in the Council of States?

options.A: Ticino, Jura and Geneva
options.B: Glarus, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Obwalden
options.C: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Basel Landschaft
options.D: Valais, Uri and Zug

source_quote: The former half-cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Basel Landschaft are only entitled to one.
notes: The six are all former half-cantons; the historical reason is a leftover of the old Confederation's status. Source spells the Basel cantons without hyphens.

question: To force an optional referendum against a law passed by the Swiss Parliament, how many valid signatures must be collected, and within what deadline?

options.A: 100,000 signatures within 100 days
options.B: 50,000 signatures within 18 months
options.C: 100,000 signatures within 18 months
options.D: 50,000 signatures within 100 days

source_quote: collect 50,000 valid signatures within 100 days of the publication of the new legislation
notes: Pair with K011: the optional referendum is 50,000 signatures / 100 days; the federal popular initiative is 100,000 / 18 months.

question: A campaign team is gathering signatures for an optional referendum against a federal law. Which restriction applies to the individual signature lists?

options.A: Each list must carry at least 500 signatures from one and the same canton.
options.B: A single list may only contain signatures from people of the same commune, because the communes are the first to check the signatures.
options.C: A voter may sign only one list per canton, and any duplicate signature invalidates the whole list.
options.D: Each list must be countersigned by the mayor of the commune before it can be submitted.

source_quote: A further requirement is that any given signature list may contain only the signatures of persons from the same commune – because the communes are the first to check the signatures.
notes: Counter-intuitive administrative detail: signature gathering is decentralised to the commune for verification. The same per-commune form rule applies to popular initiatives.

question: The voting age in Switzerland is 18 at federal level, and each canton is free to set its own age for cantonal and communal votes. Where may 16- and 17-year-olds vote?

options.A: In Glarus, at cantonal and communal level — they may vote but not stand for election.
options.B: Nowhere, because no canton may set the voting age below 18.
options.C: In Glarus, Bern and Basel-Stadt, but only in cantonal and not in communal votes.
options.D: In any canton that chooses to allow it, since cantons are entirely free to set the age.

source_quote: Currently Glarus is the only canton to allow 16- and 17-year-olds to vote at cantonal and communal level, but not to stand for election.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE and time-specific: Glarus is named as the sole canton on the page as accessed 2026-10-12. Canton is named explicitly in the stem.

question: In Switzerland the separation of powers applies at federal, cantonal and communal level. May one person hold office in more than one of the three branches of the Swiss state at the same time?

options.A: Yes, but only where the second office is at communal level and is unpaid.
options.B: Yes, provided the two offices are held in two different cantons.
options.C: Yes, because judges are treated as belonging to the executive rather than to the judiciary.
options.D: No — a person may belong to only one of the three branches of the state at any one time.

source_quote: A person may belong to only one of the three branches of the state (at federal, cantonal or communal level) at any one time.
notes: Branch incompatibility. It is why a Federal Councillor cannot sit in Parliament or on the Federal Supreme Court.

question: How many valid signatures must be collected for a federal popular initiative, and within what time limit?

options.A: 50,000 signatures within 100 days
options.B: 100,000 signatures within 18 months
options.C: 100,000 signatures within 100 days
options.D: 50,000 signatures within 18 months

source_quote: For an initiative to come to fruition, it must be signed by 100,000 voters within 18 months.
notes: Direct democracy threshold. Contrast with K007: referendum 50,000 / 100 days.

question: How many members must the committee of a federal popular initiative have, and what must each of them satisfy?

options.A: At least three members, all of whom must be Swiss citizens resident in Switzerland.
options.B: At least seven members, with no upper limit on the size of the committee.
options.C: At least seven and at most twenty-seven members, each of whom is eligible to vote in Switzerland.
options.D: Between seven and twenty-seven members, at least half of whom must come from different language regions.

source_quote: The initiative committee must have at least 7 and no more than 27 members, who each must be eligible to vote in Switzerland.
notes: There is both a floor (7) and a ceiling (27) — models frequently recall only the lower bound or invent a minimum of 3.

question: Across the Swiss cantons, who presides over the cantonal government, and what does that role carry with it?

options.A: The population of the canton elects a cantonal president directly for a four-year term, with decision-making powers equal to those of the other members.
options.B: The Federal Council appoints a cantonal president for a two-year term.
options.C: The presidency passes to the longest-serving member and carries substantial additional powers.
options.D: The presidency usually rotates from year to year and carries no privileges beyond chairing the cantonal government's meetings.

source_quote: Cantonal governments usually have a different president each year - the position rotating according to the length of time the government members have been in office. The president does not enjoy any special privileges or status, apart from chairing cantonal government meetings.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE: rotation follows length of service, so the source says 'usually'. Phrased as the general cantonal pattern, never as a universal seven-member rule.

question: How does the size of a cantonal parliament vary in Switzerland? Give the two figures cited on the federal ch.ch portal.

options.A: Appenzell Innerrhoden has 50 members and Zurich has 180.
options.B: Appenzell Innerrhoden has 28 members and Zurich has 180.
options.C: Appenzell Innerrhoden has 50 members and Zurich has 200.
options.D: Every canton has 100 members, with seats assigned in proportion to population.

source_quote: The number of members of parliament varies from canton to canton. It is usually proportional to the population of the canton. The parliament of Appenzell Innerrhoden currently has 50 members while the Zurich parliament has 180 members.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE and time-specific ('currently' as of the 2026-10-12 page). Both cantons are named explicitly, per the cantonal-variation rule.

question: In Swiss popular votes, which proposals require a so-called 'double majority' rather than a simple majority of the voters?

options.A: Federal laws and most international treaties.
options.B: Amendments to the Constitution and decisions to join a supranational community.
options.C: Amendments to the Constitution only — joining a supranational community requires a popular majority alone.
options.D: Any proposal on which more than one canton votes.

source_quote: But the decision to amend the constitution or join a supranational community requires a so-called double majority. Such a proposal is accepted only if both the majority of voters (popular majority) as well as the majority of cantons say yes.
notes: The supranational-community limb is the non-obvious half — it is what would apply to any EU accession question, which Switzerland is not part of.

question: When the cantonal majority is counted for a constitutional amendment or a vote on joining a supranational community, what weight does each of the former half-cantons carry?

options.A: A full vote, the same as any other canton.
options.B: No vote at all, since they are no longer separate cantons.
options.C: Half a vote each.
options.D: Two votes each, reflecting their combined historic weight.

source_quote: The votes of the former half-cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden each count as half a vote.
notes: The six former half-cantons weigh 0.5 each, so the cantonal majority is effectively a weighted 23-canton vote. Note this is a separate mechanism from the single Council of States seat they hold.

question: Switzerland is running e-voting trials. What numerical limits apply to how many voters may use them?

options.A: Up to 30% of eligible voters in any one canton, with a national cap of 10%.
options.B: Up to 10% of eligible voters in any one canton, with a national cap of 30%.
options.C: Up to 30% of eligible voters nationwide, with no separate cantonal cap.
options.D: No numerical cap at all — each canton decides freely how many of its voters may vote online.

source_quote: The scope of the trials is limited: a maximum of 30% of eligible voters are permitted to use e-voting in any particular canton, with the national cap set at 10%.
notes: The per-canton 30% / national 10% split is inverted from the intuitive reading. As accessed 2026-10-12; actual participation falls well below these quotas.

question: Apart from the Federal Supreme Court, how many further courts exercise judicial functions at the federal level in Switzerland, and which are they?

options.A: One — the Federal Constitutional Court.
options.B: Three — the Federal Criminal Court, the Federal Administrative Court and the Federal Patent Court.
options.C: Three — the Federal Criminal Court, the Federal Constitutional Court and the Federal Supreme Administrative Court.
options.D: Two — the Federal Criminal Court and the Federal Administrative Court.

source_quote: The Federal Criminal Court, the Federal Administrative Court and the Federal Patent Court are the three other courts at federal level.
notes: There is no separate Federal Constitutional Court — a common import from Germany (Bundesverfassungsgericht) or Austria. The Federal Patent Court is the genuinely non-obvious fourth federal court.

question: About how many items of business does the Swiss Federal Council deal with in a year?

options.A: around 250
options.B: around 25,000
options.C: around 2,500
options.D: around 250,000

source_quote: Each year the Federal Council deals with around 2,500 items of business.
notes: Replaces an earlier K019 (duration of the weekly meeting), which was rejected at manual review: three of its four options were implausible. This item tests the small size of the Swiss consensus executive - seven councillors handling ~2,500 items, against the tens of thousands a large national cabinet would process. Distractors span three orders of magnitude so each is a real candidate.

question: The Federal Chancellery supports the Federal Council but is neither the head of state nor the head of government. Which of the following is one of its actual duties in Switzerland?

options.A: Chairing the Federal Council meetings and representing it abroad.
options.B: Supervising the seven federal departments and their heads.
options.C: Adjudicating appeals against decisions of the federal authorities.
options.D: Organising federal elections and referendums, as guardian of the people's rights.

source_quote: As guardian of the people's rights, the Federal Chancellery organises federal elections and referendums.
notes: Precise delimitation: the Chancellery is the Federal Council's staff office, not a head of state/government. Referendum and initiative committees submit their signatures to it.

question: In Switzerland, what is the shortest notice period that can validly be agreed for terminating a tenancy?

options.A: One month for residential premises and three months for commercial premises
options.B: Two months for residential premises and four months for commercial premises
options.C: Three months for residential premises and six months for commercial premises
options.D: Three months for residential premises only, with no statutory minimum for commercial premises

source_quote: In einem Mietvertrag muss die Kündigungsfrist mindestens drei Monate für Wohnräume und sechs Monate für Geschäftsräume betragen, es können aber auch längere Fristen vereinbart werden.
notes: Source quote is German (official Canton Bern conciliation-authority page); English rendering in the question: in a rental agreement the notice period must be at least three months for residential premises and six months for commercial premises, and longer periods may be agreed. Commonly cited German practice of one month's notice plus end-of-month termination is NOT the Swiss rule.

question: A tenant in Switzerland posts their notice of termination on 31 March, and the landlord receives it on 1 April. From when does the notice period run, and when does the termination take effect?

options.A: It runs from 31 March, the date the notice was posted, so the termination takes effect at the end of June
options.B: It runs from 1 April, the date the notice is delivered to the landlord, so the termination takes effect at the end of July
options.C: It runs from 1 April, the date of delivery, so the termination takes effect at the end of June
options.D: It runs from the first day of the calendar month after delivery, so the termination takes effect at the end of August

source_quote: Die Kündigungsfrist läuft erst ab Zustellung der Kündigung an die Vermieterin oder den Vermieter. Wenn Sie also beispielsweise am 31. März die Kündigung verschicken und die Vermieterin oder der Vermieter diese am 1. April erhält, gilt die Kündigung erst auf Ende Juli statt Ende Juni.
notes: German source; English rendering: the notice period only begins on delivery of the notice to the landlord — sent 31 March and received 1 April, it takes effect at the end of July rather than the end of June. Posting date is not decisive.

question: A married couple lives in a Swiss flat, but only one of the spouses is named as the tenant on the rental agreement. Who must sign the letter terminating the tenancy?

options.A: Both spouses must sign the termination, even though only one of them is named as the tenant on the rental agreement
options.B: Only the spouse named as tenant must sign, because only that person is a contracting party
options.C: Only the named tenant signs, but only after obtaining the written consent of the other spouse
options.D: Either spouse may sign alone, and the landlord must accept either signature

source_quote: Wenn Sie als Ehepaar oder eingetragene Partner/innen in der Wohnung wohnen, müssen beide die Kündigung unterschreiben. Dies gilt auch dann, wenn nur eine/r von Ihnen auf dem Mietvertrag als Mieter/in aufgeführt ist.
notes: German source; English rendering: couples who live in the flat as spouses or registered partners must both sign the termination, and this applies even if only one of them is listed as tenant on the rental agreement. Covers registered partners as well as married couples.

question: An EU/EFTA citizen takes a job in Switzerland on an employment contract of unlimited duration. Which Swiss residence permit are they issued, and for how long is it valid?

options.A: An L short-term residence permit, valid for the term of the employment contract
options.B: A C settlement permit, valid for five years
options.C: A G cross-border commuter permit, valid for five years
options.D: A B residence permit, valid for five years

source_quote: The residence permit for EU/EFTA nationals is valid for five years. This permit is issued to EU/EFTA citizens holding a contract of employment of at least twelve months or of unlimited duration.
notes: Switzerland applies its own permit categories to EU/EFTA nationals under the free movement agreement; it is in Schengen but not in the EU, so the EU directive-style permit nomenclature does not apply.

question: For which duration of employment contract is an EU/EFTA national entitled to the Swiss short-term residence permit (category L)?

options.A: A contract of one to three months
options.B: A contract of three to twelve months
options.C: A contract of twelve to twenty-four months
options.D: A contract of twelve months or unlimited duration

source_quote: EU/EFTA nationals are entitled to this permit provided they are in possession of an employment contract valid from three up to twelve months.
notes: The Swiss L permit is defined by the employment-contract term, not by a 90-day short-stay rule as in EU free-movement law. Contracts of under three months within a calendar year need no permit at all, only the online notification procedure (separate fact, not tested here).

question: After five years of regular and uninterrupted residence in Switzerland, which nationals are granted settlement permits pursuant to settlement treaties or reciprocal agreements?

options.A: All nationals of all EU and EFTA member states, once they have completed five years' residence
options.B: Only EFTA nationals — Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway
options.C: Nationals of Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden, as well as EFTA nationals (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway)
options.D: Only nationals of the EU member states that acceded to the EU most recently

source_quote: If they meet the required conditions, nationals of Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden as well as EFTA nationals (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway) are granted settlement permits pursuant to settlement treaties or reciprocal agreements after five years' regular and uninterrupted residence in Switzerland.
notes: Switzerland holds bilateral settlement agreements with 15 EU states plus the three EFTA states; the source states expressly that no such treaties exist for the nationals of the other EU member states. SEM sets the earliest date from which settlement permits may be granted.

question: A holder of a Swiss EU/EFTA cross-border commuter permit (category G) lives in a neighbouring EU state and works in Switzerland. How often must they return to their main place of residence abroad?

options.A: As a rule every day, or at least once a week
options.B: At least once a month
options.C: At least once every six months
options.D: Only when the permit is renewed or its validity is extended

source_quote: Cross-border commuters must return to their main place of residence abroad as a rule every day, or at least once a week.
notes: Category G has no direct EU equivalent; it is the Swiss instrument for EU/EFTA nationals who live abroad and work in Switzerland, whether employed or self-employed.

question: Under Swiss federal law, what residence requirement must be met before applying for ordinary naturalisation?

options.A: At least five years of residence, including one of the two years preceding the application
options.B: At least ten years of residence, all of it within the five years preceding the application
options.C: At least fifteen years of residence, including five of the ten years preceding the application
options.D: At least ten years of residence, including three of the five years prior to the application being made

source_quote: Federal law requires you to have lived in Switzerland for at least ten years, including three of the five years prior to the application being made.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE: on top of the federal ten-year rule, each canton sets an additional requirement of between two and five years' residence in the particular commune or canton, and each commune makes its own rules within cantonal and federal law. Those extra conditions are deliberately not tested here.

question: For ordinary naturalisation in Switzerland, how is time spent in Switzerland between the ages of 8 and 18 treated, and when can the applicant first apply?

options.A: It counts once, and no application is possible until at least ten years of total residence
options.B: It counts double, but no application is possible until at least six years of total residence in the country
options.C: It counts double, but no application is possible until at least twelve years of total residence
options.D: It counts double, but no application is possible before the applicant reaches the age of 18

source_quote: The time spent in Switzerland between the ages of 8 and 18 counts double, but you cannot apply for naturalisation until you have lived in the country for at least six years.
notes: The six-year floor is the earliest any application may be made and is a separate condition from the ten-year federal requirement tested in K028.

question: Which Swiss residence permit must a foreign citizen already hold before being able to apply for ordinary naturalisation?

options.A: A short-term residence permit (L)
options.B: A residence permit (B)
options.C: A settlement permit (C)
options.D: A cross-border commuter permit (G)

source_quote: Holders of a settlement permit (C permit)
notes: Ordinary naturalisation is restricted to holders of a C permit; the residency periods themselves are tested separately. Simplified naturalisation is open to other categories (spouse or child of a Swiss citizen, stateless minor, third-generation residents under 25).

question: How long is a Swiss provisional (learner) driving licence valid for category B (cars), compared with category A (motorcycles)?

options.A: 12 months for cars and 6 months for motorcycles
options.B: 24 months for cars and for motorcycles alike
options.C: 36 months for cars and 12 months for motorcycles
options.D: 24 months for cars and 4 months for motorcycles

source_quote: The provisional licence is valid for 24 months for cars (category B) and for 4 months for motorcycles (category A).
notes: The motorcycle figure is strikingly short compared with the car figure; the provisional licence is also valid only in Switzerland.

question: In Switzerland, what conditions must a person meet in order to accompany a learner driver on a drive?

options.A: They must be at least 23 years old, have passed their driving test at least three years previously, and no longer hold a probationary driving licence
options.B: They must be at least 21 years old and have held a full driving licence for at least one year
options.C: They must be at least 25 years old and have held a full category B licence for at least five years
options.D: They must be at least 18 years old, provided they have not been disqualified from driving in the previous two years

source_quote: The accompanying person must be at least 23 years old, have passed their driving test at least three years previously and must no longer have a probationary driving licence.
notes: Three cumulative conditions: age, three years since passing the driving test, and no longer being on a probationary licence. Learner drivers may not have drunk alcohol before driving; the legal limit is a blood alcohol level of over 0.01%.

question: A learner obtains a Swiss provisional driving licence on their 19th birthday. How long must they wait before they may take the practical driving test?

options.A: Six months
options.B: At least twelve months
options.C: At least twenty-four months
options.D: No fixed waiting period, once the compulsory traffic skills course has been attended

source_quote: If you get your provisional licence before your 20th birthday, you will need to wait at least 12 months before you can take the practical driving test.
notes: The 12-month wait is conditional on the provisional licence having been issued before the 20th birthday; the compulsory eight-hour traffic skills course is a separate precondition for registering for the test.

question: In Switzerland, on which tax bases do the three taxing levels — the Confederation, the cantons and the communes — levy taxes on private individuals?

options.A: All three levels levy taxes on both income and assets
options.B: The Confederation taxes income only, the cantons tax assets only, and the communes tax both income and assets
options.C: The Confederation taxes assets only, while the cantons and communes tax income only
options.D: The Confederation levies direct federal tax on income, while the cantons and communes levy taxes on both income and assets

source_quote: The cantons and the communes levy their taxes on both the income and the assets of private individuals.
notes: The page deliberately carries no CHF figures, rates or brackets; the Confederation taxes income only, whereas the two sub-national levels tax income and wealth. No rate may be presented as a nationwide figure.

question: Two neighbouring communes in the same Swiss canton can levy different tax rates on an identical household income. What accounts for the difference?

options.A: Each commune determines its own tax co-efficient, and these co-efficients can vary considerably
options.B: Each canton sets a separate statutory tax rate for each individual commune within it
options.C: The Confederation adds a municipal surtax that differs from commune to commune
options.D: The statutory tax rate is fixed by federal law but is waived by individual communes

source_quote: Because each commune determines its own tax co-efficient, and these can vary considerably, there can be low-tax and high-tax communes within the same canton.
notes: COMMUNAL-VARIABLE: the co-efficient is changed from time to time, so no specific value is permanent. This is why there can be low-tax and high-tax communes within a single canton — a distinctly Swiss feature of communal tax autonomy.

question: What is the minimum annual holiday entitlement for a worker in Switzerland who is under 20 years old?

options.A: Four weeks
options.B: Three weeks
options.C: Five weeks
options.D: Six weeks

source_quote: Up to the age of 20, you are entitled to at least five weeks' vacation.
notes: The general statutory minimum for all workers is four weeks regardless of full- or part-time; the entitlement rises to at least five weeks up to the age of 20, and more may be agreed. Distinct from the public-holiday facts carried by S031.

question: In Switzerland, may an employee decide unilaterally when to take their statutory annual leave?

options.A: Yes — the statutory entitlement is unconditional, so the employee alone fixes the dates
options.B: No — the employer must approve the time off, and may require the employee to change dates that are not compatible with the needs or interests of the company
options.C: No — leave may only be taken in the calendar year in which it was earned
options.D: Yes, provided one month's notice is given to the employer in advance

source_quote: You need your employer's approval to take time off. If your holidays are not compatible with the needs or interests of the company, your boss can ask you to change them.
notes: This is the fact that appears on S013 but not on the shared S031 page; keeping it here avoids duplicating the public-holiday facts.

question: For a residential rental in Switzerland, what is the maximum rental deposit (security deposit) a landlord may require?

options.A: One month's rent
options.B: Two months' rent
options.C: Three months' rent
options.D: There is no statutory maximum

source_quote: Rental deposit, also known as a security deposit: This must only be paid when required in the agreement. For residential rentals, this is a maximum of three months' rent.
notes: The deposit may be demanded only if the agreement provides for it; three months' rent is a ceiling, not an entitlement.

question: What biometric data does the microchip in a Swiss biometric residence permit for foreign nationals store, and for how long?

options.A: One digital fingerprint and a facial image, stored for five years
options.B: Two digital fingerprints and a facial image, stored for ten years
options.C: A facial image and the holder's passport number, stored for three years
options.D: Two digital fingerprints and a facial image, stored for five years

source_quote: an embedded microchip with biometric data: two digital fingerprints and a facial image. The data are stored for five years and may only be used for the purpose of issuing a new biometric residence permit without the need for additional data processing.
notes: The stored data may be used only to issue a new biometric residence permit. The chip does not allow a person to be located or monitored. CANTONAL-VARIABLE: application and issuance are decided by the canton of residence.

question: When did Switzerland sign the Schengen Agreement, and when was a microchip for storing biometric data added to the new credit-card-format residence permit?

options.A: Switzerland signed the Schengen Agreement on 12 December 2008, and the microchip was added in early 2011
options.B: Switzerland signed the Schengen Agreement on 12 December 2008, and the microchip was added in 2009
options.C: Switzerland acceded to the Schengen acquis in 2004, and the microchip was added in early 2011
options.D: Switzerland signed the Schengen Agreement on 15 March 2008, and the microchip was added in early 2013

source_quote: When it signed the Schengen Agreement on 12 December 2008, Switzerland began issuing a new residence permit in credit-card format to foreign nationals. In a subsequent development in early 2011, a microchip was added to these residence permits for the purpose of storing biometric data.
notes: Switzerland joined Schengen in 2008 while remaining outside the EU and the EEA. Presented with a valid national passport, the biometric residence permit entitles the holder to travel throughout the Schengen area without a visa.

question: Switzerland's old-age insurance system is built on a three-pillar structure. Which combination correctly names the three pillars?

options.A: State provision (OASI) and occupational provision (pension funds) only
options.B: State provision, occupational provision, private provision, and a fourth universal pillar for low-income households
options.C: State provision (OASI), occupational provision (pension funds) and private provision
options.D: State provision (OASI), mandatory employer pensions and mandatory private savings for every employee

source_quote:
The Swiss old-age insurance system is based on three pillars: state provision (OASI),
occupational provision (pension funds) and private provision.
notes: Swiss-specific: the AHV / BVG / Pillar-3a triad has no direct EU equivalent. Germany has state plus occupational pensions only and no third pillar.

question: A person who has just moved to Switzerland and is not yet enrolled with a Swiss health insurer must arrange compulsory basic health insurance cover within what period?

options.A: Within one month of arriving
options.B: Within two months of arriving
options.C: Within six months of arriving
options.D: Within three months of arriving

source_quote: If you have just moved to Switzerland, you have three months in which to arrange
notes: The same three-month deadline applies to new-borns, and the person or baby is already insured during that period. This is a Swiss KVG rule, not an EU social-security coordination rule (do not import the EU three-month rule or the EU residence-condition logic).

question: In Switzerland, a policyholder who wants to switch compulsory basic health insurer for the following calendar year must have the cancellation letter received by their current insurer by which date?

options.A: 15 October
options.B: 30 November
options.C: 15 December
options.D: 31 December

source_quote: Your letter must reach your current health insurer by 30 November.
notes: The 'Stichtag 30. November' is uniquely Swiss. Note the separate mid-year cancellation right that only holders of the CHF 300 standard deductible enjoy (tested separately in this category).

question: In Switzerland, a healthy adult who chooses the highest available compulsory basic health insurance deductible should set aside how much per year in order to be able to cover their own maximum share of healthcare costs?
source_quote:
You should still put CHF 3,200 aside in case you do fall ill
(CHF 2,500 deductible and CHF 700 retention fee).
notes: CHF 3,200 = highest adult deductible CHF 2,500 + CHF 700 maximum annual retention fee. A German/EU reader is likely to think only of a deductible.

question: Under Swiss compulsory basic health insurance, an adult holds the standard annual deductible of CHF 300. What is the maximum that this adult can end up paying out of pocket for healthcare in one calendar year?

options.A: CHF 700

source_quote: In other words, for an insured person with an annual deductible of CHF 300, the maximum cost share is CHF 1000 per calendar year.
notes: Key anti-trap item: CHF 1,000 is the MAXIMUM ANNUAL COST SHARE (CHF 300 deductible + CHF 700 maximum retention fee), not a deductible band. Distractor A is the retention-fee cap alone.

question: In Swiss compulsory basic health insurance, which set of optional annual deductible levels may adults choose from?
source_quote: For adults, the available deductibles are 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500 francs, and for children 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 and 600 francs.
notes: Levels are chosen voluntarily; there is no age / income ('affluence') / rural-residence rule assigning a band. Distractor B is the children's list.

question: Under Swiss compulsory basic health insurance, a policyholder wants to raise their deductible to CHF 1,500. Which statement correctly describes the insurer's legal obligation here?

options.A: The insurer must offer the CHF 1,500 level, because it is one of the standard adult deductible levels
options.B: The insurer is not required to offer the full range of deductible levels and may offer only some of them
options.C: The insurer must offer it, but only if the policyholder is under 25 years old
options.D: The insurer must offer it, but may charge an additional administration fee

source_quote: The health insurer does not have to offer the full range of deductibles.
notes: Insurers MAY also differentiate for young adults aged 19-25. Corrects the widespread misconception that Swiss deductible levels are assigned by rule.

question: A Swiss compulsory health insurance policyholder opts for a deductible higher than the standard CHF 300, which reduces his premium. The premium reduction is capped by law at what share of the additional risk the policyholder assumes?

options.A: 70 per cent
options.B: 50 per cent
options.C: 90 per cent
options.D: 100 per cent

source_quote: A maximum of 70 percent reduction on the additional risk assumed by the policyholder may be granted.
notes: Statutory ceiling on the additional-risk discount. It is a separate rule from the statutory minimum-premium floor and must not be conflated with it.

question: Swiss law requires every compulsory health insurer to charge a floor below which the premium may not fall. What is that statutory minimum premium set at, relative to the premium the insurer would ordinarily charge?

options.A: 30 per cent of the ordinary premium with accident cover for the relevant age group and premium region
options.B: 70 per cent of the ordinary premium with accident cover for the relevant age group and premium region
options.C: 80 per cent of the ordinary premium with accident cover for the relevant age group and premium region
options.D: 50 per cent of the ordinary premium with accident cover for the relevant age group and premium region

source_quote: The health insurer is required to charge a minimum premium equivalent to 50 per cent of the ordinary premium with accident cover for the age group and premium region of the person concerned.
notes: The floor cannot be undercut even by policies excluding accident cover or restricting the choice of service provider. Prevents insurers competing on restricted-benefit products.

question: In Swiss compulsory basic health insurance, a policyholder wants to move from the standard CHF 300 deductible to a higher optional deductible. When can that change take effect?

options.A: At any time during the year, on 30 days' notice
options.B: Only at the beginning of a calendar year
options.C: From 1 April, when insurers recalculate their premiums
options.D: Immediately, provided the policyholder has had no treatment in the current year

source_quote: A change in the level of the deductible can only take effect at the beginning of a calendar year.
notes: The deductible level is locked to the calendar year, unlike, for example, switching insurers. Do not confuse with the separate end-of-June cancellation right for CHF 300 deductible holders (S019).

question: A holder of the CHF 300 deductible under a 'regular' insurance model in Switzerland wants to leave their current compulsory basic health insurer outside the ordinary year-end round. When can the cancellation take effect, and on what notice?

options.A: End of March, on one month's notice
options.B: End of July, on three months' notice
options.C: End of June, on three months' notice
options.D: End of September, on six months' notice

source_quote: cancel your basic insurance with effect from the end of June. A three-month notice period
notes: This mid-year cancellation window is tied specifically to holding the CHF 300 standard deductible; it is an exception to the ordinary 30 November deadline. No foreign analogue exists.

question: In Switzerland, a daily contribution towards the cost of a hospital stay is payable by the patient. Which groups are exempt from that contribution?

options.A: Children, young adults in education and training, and pregnant women
options.B: Children and pensioners
options.C: Everyone under the age of 25
options.D: Only women receiving maternity-related services

source_quote:
Children, young adults in education and training
and pregnant women do not pay any contribution to hospital costs.
notes: The contribution itself is CHF 15 per day. Distractor C over-extends the 'young adults in education and training' exemption (which is not simply 'under 25').

question: In Switzerland, an employee is unable to work because of an accident. From when, and at what level, is an accident daily allowance payable?

options.A: From the first day after the accident, at 100 per cent of salary
options.B: From the third day after the accident, at 80 per cent of salary
options.C: From the eighth day after the accident, at 90 per cent of salary
options.D: From the fifteenth day after the accident, at 80 per cent of salary

source_quote:
as of the third day following your
accident you are entitled to a daily allowance corresponding to 80% of your salary.
notes: Swiss UVG accident insurance. If the insurer's allowance is below 80%, the employer must make up the difference. German sickness-benefit schedules (e.g. the 6-week Lohnfortzahlung) are not the relevant frame.

question: In Switzerland, a person works 5 hours a week for an employer and is covered by the compulsory accident insurance scheme. What does that accident cover include?

options.A: Occupational accidents and occupational illnesses only; accidents during leisure time are not covered
options.B: Occupational accidents and occupational illnesses as well as non-occupational accidents occurring in leisure time
options.C: No accident cover at all, because anyone working under eight hours a week must insure privately
options.D: All accidents, including those during private leisure activities

source_quote: If you work for less than eight hours a week for your employer, your accident insurance
notes: The 8-hours-per-week threshold is the UVG dividing line: at or above it, leisure-time accidents are also covered. Accidents on the way to and from work count as occupational. This is a Swiss statutory test, not an EU social-security coordination rule.

question: Under Swiss compulsory accident insurance, what minimum degree of disability must be assessed before an injured person can qualify for an accident disability pension?

options.A: At least 5 per cent
options.B: At least 20 per cent
options.C: At least 10 per cent
options.D: At least 70 per cent

source_quote:
You must be classified as at least
10% disabled to qualify.
notes: The accident disability pension may be awarded in addition to a pension under the state IV/AI disability scheme. Distractor D (70%) is the separate BVG exclusion threshold for compulsory occupational pension cover.

question: According to the Federal Social Insurance Office, what was the maximum annual tax-deductible Pillar 3a contribution in 2025 for a self-employed person who has compulsory occupational pension (BVG) cover?
source_quote: - CHF 7,258 for employees/self-employed persons with occupational pension cover;
notes: TIME-SENSITIVE: figure explicitly labelled 2025, so the year is stated in the stem. For a person WITHOUT occupational cover the 2025 limit is 20% of earnings up to CHF 36,288. Distractors B and C are BVG entry-threshold figures from other years, not Pillar 3a limits.

question: Under the AVS/AHV 21 reform in force in Switzerland since 1 January 2024, the ordinary retirement age for women is being raised in three-month steps by birth cohort. What reference age applies to a woman born in 1962?

options.A: 64 years and 6 months
options.B: 64 years and 3 months
options.C: 64 years and 9 months
options.D: 65 years

source_quote: - women born in 1962: 64 years and 6 months;
notes: TIME-SENSITIVE and cohort-locked: born 1961 = 64y3m, 1962 = 64y6m, 1963 = 64y9m, born 1964 or later = 65. The reference age is 65 for men and for women born 1964 or later; the former general women's age of 64 is superseded and must never be presented as the current rule.

question: Under the Swiss compulsory occupational pension (2nd pillar), a member's accumulated old-age assets are converted into an annual old-age pension using a conversion factor that applies identically to men and women. What is that conversion factor?
source_quote: basis of a conversion factor of 6,80% for men and women.
notes: Swiss decimal-comma notation. A single gender-neutral conversion factor is a distinctive feature of the reformed BVG and has no direct EU analogue.

question: In Switzerland, what is the maternity allowance during the 14 weeks of maternity leave following a birth?

options.A: 80 per cent of the mother's earnings, with no upper daily limit
options.B: 90 per cent of the mother's earnings, but no more than CHF 300 per day
options.C: 80 per cent of the mother's earnings, but no more than CHF 220 per day
options.D: 100 per cent of the mother's earnings, but no more than CHF 220 per week

source_quote:
Maternity allowance amounts to 80% of your
earnings, but no more than CHF 220 per day.
notes: Highly Swiss-specific 14-week / 80% / CHF 220-per-day package. Cantonal provisions, personnel regulations and collective employment contracts may provide more generous arrangements. Do not substitute EU maternity-benefit rates.

question: How does Swiss second-parent (co-parental) leave differ from maternity leave in the way it may be taken?

options.A: It must be taken as one uninterrupted block within three months of the child's birth
options.B: It is flexible: it may be taken all at once or as individual days, but must be taken within two years of the child's birth
options.C: It must be taken in full before the mother returns to work
options.D: It is flexible: it may be taken all at once or as individual days, but must be taken within six months of the child's birth

source_quote:
Unlike maternity leave, paternity/co-parental leave is flexible. You can take
it all at once, or as individual days as long as it is taken within the
notes: Co-parental leave runs for two weeks: 14 daily allowances and ten days off work, paid at 80% of earnings capped at CHF 220/day. It must be used within six months of the birth.

question: How many national languages does Switzerland have, and what are they?

options.A: Three — German, French and Italian
options.B: Four — German, French, Italian and Romansh
options.C: Four — German, French, Italian and English
options.D: Five — German, French, Italian, Romansh and English

source_quote: Since 1938 Romansh has been recognised in the Swiss Constitution as a national language along with German, French and Italian.
notes: The 'four national languages' count must not be confused with the three official languages of the Confederation; the Romansh semi-official status is tested separately at K075.

question: Which four cantons of Switzerland are French-speaking?

options.A: Geneva, Jura, Neuchâtel and Vaud
options.B: Geneva, Jura, Neuchâtel and Valais
options.C: Geneva, Ticino, Neuchâtel and Vaud
options.D: Vaud, Valais, Fribourg and Geneva

source_quote: Four cantons are French-speaking: Geneva, Jura, Neuchâtel and Vaud.
notes: Named-canton item. Valais and Fribourg are bilingual (not monoliguously French); Ticino is Italian-speaking.

question: Is English an official language of Switzerland?

options.A: Yes — English became an official language of the Confederation in the 1938 constitutional revision that also recognised Romansh
options.B: Yes — English is an official language of the Confederation alongside German, French and Italian
options.C: No — it is not an official language, although it is widely used to bridge the country's linguistic divides
options.D: No — it is not an official language and is used in Switzerland only in the tourism sector

source_quote: Although it is not an official language, English is often used to bridge the divides, and a significant proportion of official documentation is available in English.
notes: Switzerland is not in the EU, and English has no federal status of any kind; the source is SWI swissinfo.ch quoted in the S047 file.

question: What is the lowest point in Switzerland, and in which canton is it located?

options.A: Lake Constance, in the canton of Thurgau, at 395 m
options.B: Lake Maggiore (Ticino), at 193 m
options.C: The Rhine gorge in the canton of Schaffhausen, at 302 m
options.D: Lake Neuchâtel, in the canton of Neuchâtel, at 372 m

source_quote: Lowest point: Lake Maggiore (Ticino) 193 m (633 feet)
notes: German-language readers often assume Lake Constance (Bodensee) is Switzerland's lowest point. The lowest point lies in Italian-speaking Ticino.

question: Which is the newest canton of Switzerland, and how did it come into being?

options.A: Jura — admitted to the Confederation by a national vote in 1979 after splitting off from Bern
options.B: Ticino — admitted to the Confederation by a national vote in 1803 after splitting off from Lombardy
options.C: Graubünden — admitted to the Confederation by a national vote in 1803 after splitting off from Tyrol
options.D: Jura — admitted to the Confederation by a national vote in 1848 after splitting off from Bern

source_quote: The newest canton, Jura, was admitted to the Confederation by a national vote in 1979. It split off from Bern
notes: Jura is both the newest canton and one of the four French-speaking cantons (see K062). The distractor D confuses 1979 with 1848, the year Switzerland became a federal state.

question: Switzerland shares a land border with five countries. Which of them accounts for the longest stretch of Swiss border?

options.A: France — 573 km
options.B: Italy — 740 km
options.C: Germany — 334 km
options.D: Austria — 164 km

source_quote: Borders: altogether: 1852 km/Austria 164 km/France 573 km/Germany 334 km/Italy 740 km/Liechtenstein 41 km
notes: Total border length 1,852 km; Liechtenstein is the shortest at 41 km. Per-country border lengths vary by measurement/border-survey basis (registry note).

question: Apart from the canton of Ticino, in which part of Switzerland is Italian spoken?

options.A: In four southern valleys of the canton of Graubünden
options.B: In four southern valleys of the canton of Valais
options.C: In two southern valleys of the canton of Ticino and around the city of Lugano
options.D: In the Italian-speaking minority areas of the cantons of Fribourg and Geneva

source_quote: Italian is spoken in Ticino and four southern valleys of Canton Graubünden.
notes: Same source file flags this fact REGIONAL VARIABLE (language shares are population-statistics dependent); the named location itself is stable. Distinct from the Graubünden trilingual-canton fact.

question: According to the Swiss federal information portal, approximately what share of the population primarily speaks (Swiss-)German as its main language?

options.A: 0.5 per cent
options.B: 8 per cent
options.C: 23 per cent
options.D: 62 per cent

source_quote: 62 per cent of the population primarily speak (Swiss-)German, 23 per cent French, 8 per cent Italian and 0.5 per cent Romansh.
notes: Distractors are the neighbouring shares in the same sentence (French / Italian / Romansh) — the classic mix-up. Figures are rounded; Switzerland Tourism (S028) gives 62.6 % German, 22.9 % French, 8.2 % Italian, 0.5 % Romansh. Shares are population-statistics dependent and REGIONAL VARIABLE.

question: Under Switzerland's National Fiscal Equalisation system, how many cantons are net contributors, and how many receive equalisation payments?

options.A: 9 cantons are net contributors; the remaining 17 cantons receive equalisation payments
options.B: 17 cantons are net contributors; the remaining 9 cantons receive equalisation payments
options.C: 13 cantons are net contributors; the remaining 13 cantons receive equalisation payments
options.D: 9 cantons are net contributors; the remaining 16 cantons receive equalisation payments

source_quote: The federal government and nine of the cantons are net contributors: ZH, SZ, OW, NW, ZG, BS, SH, AI, GE. The remaining 17 cantons receive equalisation payments (net beneficiaries).
notes: REGIONAL VARIABLE: the source file flags this fact as year-dependent. The nine net-contributor cantons are Zürich, Schwyz, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Zug, Basel-Stadt, Schaffhausen, Appenzell Innerrhoden and Geneva. The federal government is also a net contributor, so the question asks about cantons only.

question: According to SWI swissinfo.ch, how many municipalities (communes) did Switzerland have as of 1 January 2025, and what trend explains the change?

options.A: 2,121 municipalities; the number is rising because new communes are being created
options.B: 2,121 municipalities; the number is falling because communes are being merged to improve administrative efficiency
options.C: 2,100 municipalities; the number has remained more or less constant for over two centuries
options.D: 2,121 municipalities; the number is falling because communes are being dissolved into their cantons

source_quote: As of January 1, 2025, there are 2,121 municipalities.
notes: Trap 1 — the figure is date-specific. ch.ch (S025) rounds to 'around 2,100' and CH Info (S029) gives 2,110; all describe the same declining total at different reference dates. The merger trend is in the preceding sentence of the same file.

question: How many members does a cantonal government in Switzerland have, and how is it chosen?

options.A: Three to five members, appointed by the federal parliament
options.B: Five to seven members, appointed by the cantonal parliament
options.C: Nine members, elected by the people
options.D: Five to seven members, elected by the people

source_quote: Cantonal governments have five to seven members and are elected by the people.
notes: Cantonal variation is the point: the size of a cantonal executive is not fixed, which is why no single federal figure exists. The same source notes cantonal parliaments are unicameral and named differently in each canton.

question: Roughly what proportion of Swiss communes have their own parliament?

options.A: Around a fifth
options.B: Around a third
options.C: Around a half
options.D: Around a tenth

source_quote: Around a fifth of Switzerland's communes have their own parliaments, and local laws relating to matters such as streets, school buildings, water and energy prices, as well as parking regulations.
notes: Where a commune has no parliament, the commune assembly decides in its place — the source page does not state this, so it is not asserted here.

question: Communes are the smallest political units in Switzerland. Which of the following is an example of a power that communes exercise as delegated by the federal and cantonal governments?

options.A: Adjudicating criminal cases at first instance
options.B: Fixing the rates of federal income taxes approved by the Federal Assembly
options.C: Maintaining a register of the resident population and ensuring civil protection
options.D: Issuing cantonal constitutions, which must be approved by the federal parliament

source_quote: They exercise the powers delegated to them by the federal and cantonal governments, such as maintaining a register of the resident population and ensuring civil protection.
notes: Distractors are all level-confusion errors (a cantonal, a federal, and a cantonal-constitutional task presented as communal powers).

question: What is the highest point in Switzerland, and in which mountain range is it located?

options.A: Dufour Peak, 4,634 m, in the Bernese Alps
options.B: Monte Rosa, 4,634 m, in the Pennine Alps
options.C: The Jungfrau, 4,158 m, in the Monte Rosa Mountains
options.D: Dufour Peak, 4,634 m, in the Monte Rosa Mountains

source_quote: Highest point: Dufour Peak, in the Monte Rosa Mountains, 4,634 m (15,203 feet)
notes: German- and Austrian-language readers commonly assume the Bernese Alps (Jungfrau/Zermatt area). The peak sits in the Monte Rosa massif on the Italian border.

question: What is the constitutional status of Romansh at the level of the Confederation?

options.A: Romansh is one of the three fully official languages of the Confederation
options.B: Romansh is a cantonal language only, recognised by the cantons that use it but not by the Federal Constitution
options.C: Romansh is a national language and a semi-official language of the Confederation
options.D: Romansh is an official language of the Confederation, but only where a canton grants it cantonal official status

source_quote: Romansh is a national language and a semi-official language of the Confederation.
notes: Highest-value item in the set: the four-national / three-official split. The same file adds that Romansh IS official 'when communicating with persons who speak Romansh', which is why option D's cantonal-conditional framing is wrong — the condition is linguistic, not cantonal.

question: In which Swiss cantons are people's assemblies, known as Landsgemeinde, still held?

options.A: Appenzell Ausserrhoden and St. Gallen
options.B: Appenzell Innerrhoden and Glarus
options.C: Glarus and Obwalden
options.D: Appenzell Innerrhoden, Glarus and Nidwalden

source_quote: People's assemblies (Landsgemeinde) are still held in the cantons of Appenzell Innerrhoden and Glarus.
notes: A Swiss institution with no foreign analogue; models routinely name Appenzell Ausserrhoden (the other Appenzell) and the two half-cantons Obwalden and Nidwalden.

question: What is the least populous commune in Switzerland, and in which canton is it located?

options.A: Kammersrohr, in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden
options.B: Rheinau, in the canton of Zurich
options.C: Rivaz, in the canton of Vaud
options.D: Kammersrohr, in the canton of Solothurn

source_quote: The least populous is Kammersrohr in the canton of Solothurn (32 people)
notes: 32 residents. Counter-intuitive: the least populous commune is in Solothurn, not in an Appenzell or Graubünden mountain canton. Population figures are year-dependent and will drift.

question: Under Swiss federalism, which level of government is responsible for any task that does not fall within the remit of the federal government?

options.A: The communes, as the smallest political units
options.B: The Federal Assembly, through its Federal Chancellery
options.C: The cantons
options.D: An association of municipalities, in consultation with the cantons

source_quote: Any tasks that do not fall under the remit of the federal government are the responsibility of the cantons.
notes: Trap 4: residuary competence sits with the cantons, not with an EU-style supranational layer and not with the communes. In the EU the equivalent residue belongs to the member states; in Switzerland the member units are the cantons.

question: The Alps make up a large part of Switzerland's territory. Approximately what share of the country's total population lives in the Alps?

options.A: About 30 per cent
options.B: About 55 per cent
options.C: About 10 per cent
options.D: About 45 per cent

source_quote: The Alps, which make up a large part of the country in terms of area, are home to only 10% of the total population.
notes: Counter-intuitive inversion of area-versus-population; the same page gives a national density of 215 inhabitants per square kilometre. Population figure is date-dependent.

question: Which six cantons are the former half-cantons of Switzerland?

options.A: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Geneva
options.B: Schwyz, Uri, Glarus, Zug, Thurgau and Solothurn
options.C: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, St. Gallen and Basel Landschaft
options.D: Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Basel Landschaft

source_quote: The former half-cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Appenzell Ausserrhoden, Appenzell Innerrhoden, Basel Stadt and Basel Landschaft are only entitled to one.
notes: Deliberately tests only the canton-identity half of the S026 fact, framed as the 6/20 structure behind the number 26. The Council of States seat arithmetic (20 cantons with two seats, 46 seats total) is owned by the politics category via S003 and is not asked here. Canton names appear in the German forms printed on the source page.

question: How many public holidays are observed nationwide across Switzerland, and which one is it?

options.A: Exactly one — 1 August, Swiss National Day
options.B: Two — 1 January (New Year's Day) and 1 August (Swiss National Day)
options.C: Three — 1 January, 1 May (Labour Day) and 1 August (Swiss National Day)
options.D: None — Switzerland has no nationwide public holidays at all; each canton sets its own calendar entirely

source_quote: The first of August – Swiss national day – is Switzerland's only national public holiday.
notes: Distinctive because 1 January, Easter Monday, Ascension Day and 1 May are statutory holidays in neighbouring EU states but carry no nationwide status in Switzerland. The cantonal layer is covered separately in K082.

question: Beyond Switzerland's single nationwide public holiday, what is the maximum number of additional public holidays a canton may declare on its own territory?

options.A: Up to two
options.B: Up to four
options.C: Up to eight
options.D: Unlimited

source_quote: The cantons can each have up to eight additional public holidays on their territory. Public holidays can thus vary from canton to canton.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE — the holiday calendar differs by canton and within a canton by commune. Framed as a cantonal power, not a federal rule.

question: In Switzerland, a public holiday falls during an employee's annual leave. How is that day treated?

options.A: It counts against the employee's vacation entitlement, so the employee effectively loses one day of leave
options.B: It must be added to the following year's leave entitlement
options.C: It is compensated with a wage supplement of at least 25%
options.D: It does not count as a day of vacation

source_quote: If a public holiday falls during your vacation, that day does not count as a day of vacation.
notes: Distractor A is the German rule, where public holidays falling inside the leave period reduce the annual leave entitlement. Deliberate German/Austrian-import trap.

question: What is the general rule under Swiss law on working on a Sunday?

options.A: Sunday work is freely permitted for any employee who has consented to it
options.B: Sunday work is generally prohibited, and is possible only subject to a special authorisation and the employee's consent
options.C: Sunday work is generally prohibited, but a simple notification to the employer is sufficient to make it lawful
options.D: Sunday work is generally prohibited and can never be authorised, in any sector

source_quote: Working on Sundays is generally prohibited in Switzerland. However, working on Sundays is possible, subject to special authorisation and the employee's consent.
notes: D is false: the health sector, hospitality, newsstands and bakeries, theatres, cinemas and the media may work Sundays without authorisation.

question: Between which hours of the day is work prohibited by the Swiss night-work ban?
source_quote: In Switzerland, the law prohibits work between 11pm and 6am.
notes: Note the source spells the window as 11pm to 6am. No national maximum weekly working time is stated on the source pages and none is asserted here.

question: Under Swiss law, what is the maximum number of hours a night worker may work in any 10-hour period, counting breaks?

options.A: 8 hours
options.B: 10 hours
options.C: 9 hours
options.D: 11 hours

source_quote: Night workers may not work for more than 9 hours in any 10-hour period, including breaks.
notes: Unusual as a rule: the maximum is expressed as a ceiling inside a rolling window rather than as a daily hour total.

question: In Switzerland, what is the minimum daily rest period an employer must grant to an employee aged 20 or over between two working days?

options.A: 8 hours
options.B: 11 consecutive hours
options.C: 12 hours
options.D: 10 hours

source_quote: it must last at least 11 consecutive hours
notes: Distractor C is the rule for employees under 18 ('the daily rest period must always be at least 12 hours'); distractor A is the once-a-week reduction the employer may grant if the two-week average is 11 hours.

question: An employee works between 11pm and 6am on fewer than 25 nights per calendar year. What must the employer pay for those nights?

options.A: Time off equal to 10% of the night hours worked
options.B: A wage supplement of at least 10%
options.C: A wage supplement of at least 50%
options.D: A wage supplement of at least 25%

source_quote: A supplement of at least 25% must be paid for work between 11pm and 6am carried out for less than 25 nights per calendar year.
notes: Distractor A is the regime for regular night work (25 or more nights per calendar year), where the compensation is time off equal to 10% of night hours; distractor C is the 50% supplement for occasional Sunday work. Cash payment in lieu of compensatory time off is prohibited.

question: Under Swiss law, which authority must an employer approach to obtain authorisation to employ workers for occasional night work?

options.A: The competent cantonal authority
options.B: The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO)
options.C: The Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS)
options.D: The commune in which the workplace is situated

source_quote: To employ workers for occasional night work, employers must contact the competent cantonal authority to apply for authorisation.
notes: Distractor B is correct only for authorisations for regular Sunday work, which go to SECO — the cantonal/federal competence split is the point being tested.

question: In Switzerland, which level of government is responsible for compulsory education?

options.A: The Confederation, acting through a federal education ministry
options.B: The communes, which set the school system and appoint the teachers
options.C: The cantons
options.D: The cantons jointly with the Confederation, under federal supervision

source_quote: Compulsory education is the responsibility of the cantons. This is why it is important to check the information on your canton's website.
notes: Switzerland has no federal school system — the structural opposite of Germany, Austria and France. Distractor B is scope confusion: communes run individual schools, but the responsibility statement sits with the cantons.

question: How many years of compulsory schooling do children in most Swiss cantons have to attend, and how is that total made up?

options.A: 9 years in total: 7 years of primary school followed by 2 years of secondary school
options.B: 11 years in total, including the two years of kindergarten
options.C: 11 years in total: 9 years of primary school followed by 2 years of secondary school
options.D: 13 years in total: 11 years of primary school followed by 2 years of secondary school

source_quote: In most cantons, children are required to attend school for 11 years, including the two years they attend kindergarten.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE in the details. Distractor C keeps the total but wrongly moves the two kindergarten years out of primary school.

question: How is compulsory schooling normally split between primary and secondary level in Switzerland, and which canton departs from that pattern?

options.A: Eight years of primary school including kindergarten and three years of secondary; Ticino instead has seven years of primary and four years of secondary
options.B: Six years of primary and five years of secondary; Ticino instead has five years of primary and six years of secondary
options.C: Nine years of primary and two years of secondary; Ticino instead has eight years of primary and three years of secondary
options.D: Eight years of primary and three years of secondary; Ticino follows the same 8+3 split as the other cantons

source_quote: Primary school, including kindergarten, usually comprises eight years. Secondary education usually comprises three years. In Ticino, primary school lasts seven years and secondary school four years.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE — 8+3 is the usual structure and is NOT a federal rule; naming Ticino is required to keep the question unambiguous.

question: Kindergarten in Switzerland generally starts at age four, with an enrolment deadline that is usually 31 July. What does the official guidance say about that deadline?

options.A: The deadline of 31 July applies in every canton without exception
options.B: The deadline is set nationally at 15 September
options.C: The deadline is set by each individual school, so it varies from school to school within every canton
options.D: Some cantons in eastern and central Switzerland have a different cut-off date

source_quote: Some cantons in eastern and central Switzerland have a different cut-off date.
notes: CANTONAL-VARIABLE — 'most children' start at four, but the entry cut-off is not uniform. A model asserting a single national school-start rule has imported a foreign assumption.

question: Which three parties share responsibility for maintaining standards in the Swiss vocational education and training (VET) system and for ensuring an adequate number of apprenticeship places?

options.A: The Confederation, the cantons and the trade unions
options.B: The Confederation, the Cantons and professional organisations
options.C: The Confederation, the cantons and the chambers of commerce and industry
options.D: The cantons, the communes and the professional organisations

source_quote: The Confederation, the Cantons and professional organisations all contribute to maintaining the high standard of vocational education and training and strive to ensure that there is an adequate number of apprenticeship positions available.
notes: Distractor C is the German model (IHK/HWK chambers); there is no chamber tier in Swiss VET. Distractor D drops the Confederation, a deliberate scope-confusion.

question: In the Swiss VET system, which qualification follows from which programme length?

options.A: A two-year programme leads to a Federal VET Diploma; three- and four-year programmes lead to a Federal VET Certificate
options.B: A two-year programme leads to a specialised school certificate; three- and four-year programmes lead to a specialised baccalaureate
options.C: A two-year programme leads to a Federal VET Certificate; three- and four-year programmes lead to a Federal VET Diploma
options.D: Two-, three- and four-year VET programmes all lead to the same Federal VET Diploma

source_quote: Two-year VET programmes lead to the award of a Federal VET Certificate; three-year and four-year VET programmes lead to the award of a Federal VET Diploma.
notes: Distractor B belongs to the separate specialised-school route (three-year certificate, then a one-year specialised baccalaureate), which is easy to conflate with VET.

question: Roughly what share of young people in Switzerland takes the dual vocational education and training route rather than an academic upper-secondary school?

options.A: About one in four
options.B: About one in two
options.C: About three in four
options.D: About two in three

source_quote: Two-thirds of young people in Switzerland benefit from the solid foundation provided by vocational education and training.
notes: Distractor B mirrors the German apprenticeship uptake of roughly one in two. The Swiss dual-route share is markedly higher.

question: Switzerland recycles a high share of its waste, yet materials recovered from waste form only a small share of the country's total material consumption. What are the two figures?

options.A: 70% of total waste volume recycled, but secondary raw materials at 14% of total material consumption
options.B: 70% of total waste volume recycled, and secondary raw materials at 70% of total material consumption
options.C: 14% of total waste volume recycled, and secondary raw materials at 70% of total material consumption
options.D: 53% of municipal solid waste recycled, and secondary raw materials at 14% of total material consumption

source_quote: At present, over two thirds (70%) of Switzerland's total waste volume is recycled. Measured against total material consumption, materials recovered from waste (known as secondary raw materials) make up only a small proportion: 14% in 2019
notes: The 14% figure is from 2019; the 70% recycling rate is 'at present' as published by FOEN. Distractor D uses the municipal-solid-waste rate (53% in 2020), which measures a different quantity. MUNICIPAL-WASTE-VARIABLE: municipal waste figures are administered at commune level.

question: According to the Federal Office for the Environment, which of these four materials had the highest recycling rate in Switzerland in 2020?

options.A: Aluminium
options.B: PET
options.C: Glass
options.D: Paper

source_quote: Recycling focuses on established materials such as glass (recycling rate in 2020: 99%), PET (recycling rate in 2020: 82%), aluminium (recycling rate in 2020: 97%), paper (recycling rate in 2020: 82%).
notes: The published rates are glass 99%, aluminium 97%, PET 82% and paper 82%. The top two are only two points apart, so intuition about 'metal vs glass' is not sufficient — the exact figures are required.

question: A traveller returning to Switzerland carries goods for personal use with a total value of CHF 400. The tax-free import limit is CHF 150. On what amount is the Swiss import VAT calculated?

options.A: On the excess only — the CHF 250 by which the total value exceeds the CHF 150 limit
options.B: On the whole value — CHF 400
options.C: On the first CHF 150 only
options.D: On nothing, because all the goods are for personal use

source_quote: If the total value exceeds CHF 150, you must pay VAT on the total value of the imported goods. Example: The total value is CHF 400.
notes: Distractor A is the intuitive 'excess only' rule used in many other countries. The verified Swiss tax-free limit is CHF 150 per person per day.

question: What are the Swiss standard VAT rate and the reduced rate that applies to goods such as foodstuffs, books, magazines and medicines?

options.A: 6.7% standard, 2.1% reduced
options.B: 8.1% standard, 3.8% reduced
options.C: 10.0% standard, 2.6% reduced
options.D: 8.1% standard, 2.6% reduced

source_quote: VAT is 8.1%. A reduced rate of 2.6% applies for certain goods (e.g. foodstuffs, including non-alcoholic beverages, books, magazines and medicines).
notes: Distractor A is the pre-2001 Swiss rate pair. Figures as published by the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security at access date 2026-10-12.

question: The Waldstatte Alliance concluded in 1291 between Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden was sealed by which document?

options.A: the Peace of Westphalia of 1648
options.B: the Federal Charter of 1291
options.C: the Federal Treaty of 1815
options.D: the Federal Constitution of 1848

source_quote: In 1291, the three cantons of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden concluded the regional Waldstätte Alliance, which was sealed by the Federal Charter of 1291.
notes: Distractors C and D are real Swiss foundational documents, which is what makes the 1291 charter easy to confuse. Source URL is bar.admin.ch, a federal archive substitution for the blocked eda.admin.ch history page.

question: When the Helvetian Republic was proclaimed in 1798 under French occupation, which institution — described as a predecessor of today's Swiss Federal Archives — was established at the same time?

options.A: the Central Archives
options.B: the Swiss National Library
options.C: the Federal Mint
options.D: the Federal Chancellery

source_quote: The Central Archives, a predecessor of the current Swiss Federal Archives, were also established during this time.
notes: Distractors are all real Swiss federal institutions that simply do not date from 1798.

question: Switzerland's neutrality is recognised worldwide. What is Switzerland therefore often asked to do?

options.A: contribute troops to United Nations peacekeeping forces
options.B: host the headquarters of a NATO body
options.C: mediate in conflicts or exercise protective power mandates
options.D: take part in the collective defence commitments of an alliance

source_quote: Switzerland's neutrality is recognised worldwide, which is why it is often asked to mediate in conflicts or exercise protective power mandates.
notes: Mediation and protective power mandates are classic Swiss neutrality roles; the options that assume alliance or UN membership are the standard EU/NATO import error.

question: Switzerland is not a member of NATO. Within which two frameworks does it nevertheless cooperate with NATO?

options.A: the Partnership for Peace and the Western European Union
options.B: the European Union's Common Security and Defence Policy and the Western European Union
options.C: the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe and the Council of Europe
options.D: the Partnership for Peace and the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council

source_quote: Switzerland is not a member of NATO, but cooperates with it within the framework of the Partnership for Peace and the Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council.
notes: Shared page with S041; NATO non-membership plus PfP/EAPC cooperation is a specifically Swiss arrangement.

question: Under which constitutional instrument did the Swiss Federal Supreme Court become a permanent court?
